title: Layers, Ownership, and Responsibilities
readerIntent: Choose the correct layer for a change.
owner: Each Nodics module for its own business or framework capability
summary: Each layer has one primary responsibility; keeping those boundaries prevents duplicate authority, hidden coupling, and untestable customization.

sections.heading: Core layers
items: Configuration declares variable behavior and runtime selections.
Schemas describe governed data shape, relationships, access metadata, and persistence intent.
Models expose framework-managed item and search interaction rather than direct database access.
Services own reusable business or technical behavior.
Facades coordinate a use case across services while keeping controllers thin.
Controllers adapt transport requests and responses; routers declare secured API exposure.
Pipelines coordinate ordered, observable processing steps.
Interceptors extend defined lifecycle points without copying the owning process.
Events communicate completed facts or asynchronous work across capability boundaries.
Libraries and utilities contain stateless reusable mechanics, not hidden business authority.
Status definitions provide stable success and error codes; handlers map them to transport responses.

sections.heading: Ownership test
paragraphs: Ask which capability owns the rule, which layer owns that kind of responsibility, and which existing extension point already exists. A convenient call site is not necessarily the correct owner.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
items: Business logic in a frontend, controller, utility, package.json, or database adapter.
Direct persistence from a feature service instead of its schema model and service contracts.
A second loader, registry, validation route, or governance mechanism for the same authority.
Cross-module source imports that bypass the owning module API or event contract.
